newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Swedish bank merger speculation heats up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swedish bank merger speculation heats up.

text.p: Speculation about a merger between Swedish banks S-E-Banken and Nordbanken grew on Friday when a heavyweight newspaper reported that the deal could be revealed next week.
"I would think that they would probably merge this year... "If you are going to do it, there is no point in delaying," said Keith Baird, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.

Citing sources, the daily Dagens Nyheter said signs that a merger was about to happen included reports that the banks had had comprehensive discussions, put a general freeze on hiring and stopped investments.

In addition, top managers from S-E-Banken had been asked to cancel any travel plans and the board had instructed them to be prepared for any possible organisational changes at the beginning of the year, the newspaper said.
The article set the banks' shares soaring on a bearish Stockholm Stock Exchange. At 1230 GMT, Nordbanken's share was up 11 crowns at 226 ($31.33), while S-E-Banken was up 2.5 at 70.5.

Swedish banking shares have surged since early autumn 1996 on speculation about a major sector restructuring. Banking group Handelsbanken's bid for mortgage bank Stadshypotek about a month ago increased pressure on other players to act.

But several local analysts were not convinced by the newspaper report because of ownership problems, with the government having 59 percent in Nordbanken and the Wallenberg family's financial empire holding 15 percent in family bank S-E-Banken.
"The article does not confirm that the banks and the government have been in talks," said Jonny Sylven, analyst at Stockholm-based bank Swedbank.
"The banks would not want to repeat what Skandia did, that is to go behind the largest owner's back, so it is hard to take the article seriously."
Insurer Skandia and Stadshypotek proposed merging late in 1996 without support from the government, which held a 34 percent stake in Stadshypotek.
The deal failed. When Handelsbanken presented its bid in a government auction, Skandia withdrew.
Neither the finance ministry nor the banks had any comment about the newspaper article or a possible merger.

"I have nothing to say about the speculation and rumours concerning Nordbanken and S-E-Banken that are in the air today," said Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, reiterating that the state's Nordbank stake is for sale.
"But we are not in a hurry," he said, adding that the state would deal first with selling its Stadshypotek stake.
Analysts also said the government would probably sell its Nordbanken stake through an auction, which would ensure that taxpayers got the best price.
"If the government strikes a deal with Investor, it could attract critisism for not looking into other possibilities," said Fredrik Myren, analyst at HSBC James Capel in Stockholm.
Speculation has centred on a deal where the Wallenberg's key holding company Investor AB buys the state's Nordbanken stake to allow the family to control the new bank.

Furthermore, a merger would mean staff cuts, in turn aggravating unemployment, which is one of the hottest potatoes for the Swedish government as general elections are looming in the autumn of 1998, analysts said.

In the first nine months of 1996, Nordbanken posted an operating profit of 5.7 billion crowns and a return on equity of 27.2 percent. Corresponding figures for S-E-Banken were 4.42 billion and 21.6 percent. ($1=7.212 Swedish Crown)
